title: London dispersion forces
body: Coulombic interactions between temporary, fluctuating dipoles, often the strongest net intermolecular force between large molecules.
caution: Do not use "London dispersion forces" as a synonym for "van der Waals forces."
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.1 London dispersion forces are a result of the Coulombic interactions between temporary, fluctuating dipoles

title: Dipole-dipole interactions
body: Attractions between polar molecules whose strength depends on the magnitudes of the dipoles and their relative orientation, acting in addition to London dispersion forces.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.2 Dipole-dipole interactions are present between polar molecules

title: Ion-dipole forces
body: Forces of attraction between ions and polar molecules, which tend to be stronger than dipole-dipole forces.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.2 Ion-dipole forces of attraction are present between ions and polar molecules

title: Hydrogen bonding
body: A strong intermolecular interaction in which a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to N, O, or F is attracted to the negative end of a dipole on an N, O, or F atom in a different molecule or a different part of the same molecule.
caution: The hydrogen bond is the attraction between molecules (or regions), not the covalent O-H, N-H, or F-H bond itself; name the H and the N/O/F atoms involved.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.4 Hydrogen bonding is a strong type of intermolecular interaction

hooks.when_to_use: To recall which atoms the hydrogen must be bonded to for hydrogen bonding.
hooks.caution: In an answer, state that H bonded to N, O, or F is attracted to the negative end of the dipole on N, O, or F in another molecule (or region); do not just write "FON."

title: Polar vs. nonpolar molecules of similar size
body: Interactions between polar molecules are typically greater than those between nonpolar molecules of comparable size because dipole-dipole interactions act in addition to London dispersion forces.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.2 act in addition to London dispersion forces

title: Partial charges explain dipole and ion-dipole strength
body: The relative strength and orientation dependence of dipole-dipole and ion-dipole forces are explained by the sign of the partial charges and how they interact with an ion or an adjacent dipole.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.3 considering the sign of the partial charges responsible for the molecular dipole moment

title: Noncovalent interactions in large biomolecules
body: In large biomolecules, noncovalent interactions can occur between different molecules or between different regions of the same molecule, and they largely dictate molecular shape and function.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.5 / 3.2.A.7 noncovalent interactions may occur between different molecules or between different regions of the same large biomolecule

title: IMF strength vs. vapor pressure, boiling point, melting point
body: Vapor pressure and boiling point are directly related to intermolecular force strength because the interactions are completely overcome in vaporization, while melting points correlate more subtly because the interactions are only rearranged.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1 vapor pressure and boiling point are directly related to the strength of those interactions

title: Four types of solids and their properties
body: Ionic, covalent network, molecular, and metallic solids, each with characteristic particle-level structure and macroscopic properties.

items.label: Ionic
items.meaning: Strong ion-ion interactions: low vapor pressure, high melting and boiling points, brittle (like charges repel when layers slide); conducts only when ions are mobile (molten or dissolved).

items.label: Covalent network
items.meaning: Atoms covalently bonded in a 3-D network (diamond) or layers (graphite), only from nonmetals/metalloids; high melting points; 3-D networks rigid and hard; graphite soft because layers slide.

items.label: Molecular
items.meaning: Discrete covalently bonded molecules held by relatively weak intermolecular forces: low melting point, do not conduct because valence electrons are held in bonds and lone pairs.

items.label: Metallic
items.meaning: Free valence electrons: good conductors of electricity and heat, malleable and ductile; interstitial alloys are more rigid (less malleable/ductile) but still conduct.

title: Crystalline vs. amorphous solids
body: Crystalline solids have particles arranged in a regular three-dimensional structure, while amorphous solids have no regular, orderly arrangement of particles.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.1 crystalline, where the particles are arranged in a regular three-dimensional structure, or ... amorphous

title: Particulate model of solid, liquid, and gas
body: Particle diagrams distinguishing arrangement, spacing, and motion in the three phases.

items.label: Solid
items.meaning: Particles in close contact in a regular (crystalline) or irregular (amorphous) arrangement; motion limited, no overall translation.

items.label: Liquid
items.meaning: Particles in close contact (molar volume similar to solid) but continually moving and colliding.

items.label: Gas
items.meaning: Particles far apart on average and in constant motion; neither definite volume nor definite shape.

title: Ideal gas law
body: PV = nRT
ced_evidence: 3.4.A.1 EQN: PV = nRT

title: Partial pressure from mole fraction
body: P_A = P_{total} \times X_A
ced_evidence: 3.4.A.2 EQN: PA = Ptotal × XA

title: Mole fraction
body: X_A = \frac{\text{moles A}}{\text{total moles}}
ced_evidence: 3.4.A.2 where XA = moles A/total moles

title: Total pressure of a gas mixture
body: P_{total} = P_A + P_B + P_C + \ldots
ced_evidence: 3.4.A.2 EQN: Ptotal = PA + PB + PC + …

title: Kinetic energy of a particle
body: KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.2 EQN: KE = ½ mv2

title: Temperature and average kinetic energy
body: The Kelvin temperature of a sample is proportional to the average kinetic energy of its particles.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.3 The Kelvin temperature of a sample of matter is proportional to the average kinetic energy

title: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
body: A graphical representation of the distribution of particle kinetic energies (or velocities) at a given temperature.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.4 The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution provides a graphical representation

title: Causes of deviation from ideal gas behavior
body: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas law for two reasons.

items.label: Interparticle attractions
items.meaning: Particularly at conditions close to those resulting in condensation.

ced_evidence: 3.6.A.1 Deviations from the ideal gas law may result from interparticle attractions ... Deviations may also arise from particle volumes

title: Solution vs. heterogeneous mixture
body: A solution (homogeneous mixture) has macroscopic properties that do not vary throughout the sample, whereas a heterogeneous mixture has properties that depend on location.
ced_evidence: 3.7.A.1 In a solution, the macroscopic properties do not vary throughout the sample

title: Molarity
body: M = \frac{n_{solute}}{L_{solution}}
ced_evidence: 3.7.A.2 EQN: M = nsolute /Lsolution

title: Particulate representation of a solution
body: A particle drawing of a mixture showing the relative concentrations of components and the interactions among them.

items.label: Relative concentrations
items.meaning: Numbers of each component's particles drawn in proportion to their concentrations.

items.label: Interactions between components
items.meaning: Attractions drawn between particles (e.g., ion-dipole, hydrogen bonds) that explain solubility or miscibility.

ced_evidence: 3.8.A.1 Particulate representations of solutions communicate the structure and properties of solutions

title: Separating a liquid solution
body: Components of a liquid solution cannot be separated by filtration, but can be separated by processes that exploit differences in their intermolecular interactions.
ced_evidence: 3.9.A.1 The components of a liquid solution cannot be separated by filtration

title: Chromatography
body: A separation (paper, thin-layer, or column) that uses the differential strength of intermolecular interactions of the components in the mobile phase with each other and with the stationary phase, so the chromatogram shows relative polarities.
ced_evidence: 3.9.A.1 Chromatography (paper, thin-layer, and column) separates chemical species

title: Solubility and similar intermolecular interactions
body: Substances with similar intermolecular interactions tend to be miscible or soluble in one another.
ced_evidence: 3.10.A.1 Substances with similar intermolecular interactions tend to be miscible or soluble

title: Spectral region and associated transition
body: Each region of the electromagnetic spectrum is associated with a type of molecular motion or electronic transition.

title: Energy change on photon absorption or emission
body: When an atom or molecule absorbs (or emits) a photon, its energy increases (or decreases) by an amount equal to the photon's energy.
ced_evidence: 3.12.A.1 increased (or decreased) by an amount equal to the energy of the photon

title: Wavelength, frequency, and speed of light
body: c = \lambda \nu
ced_evidence: 3.12.A.2 EQN: c = λν

title: Planck's equation
body: E = h\nu
ced_evidence: 3.12.A.2 EQN: E = hν

title: Beer-Lambert law
body: A = \varepsilon b c
ced_evidence: 3.13.A.1 EQN: A = εbc

title: Molar absorptivity
body: The quantity ε that describes how intensely a chemical species absorbs light of a specific wavelength.
ced_evidence: 3.13.A.1 The molar absorptivity, ε, describes how intensely a chemical species absorbs light

title: Constant path length and wavelength
body: With path length and wavelength held constant, absorbance is proportional only to concentration, and the spectrophotometer is set to the wavelength of maximum absorbance for maximum sensitivity.
ced_evidence: 3.13.A.2 the absorbance is proportional only to the concentration of absorbing molecules or ions
